title: Define and understand production systems and production management

lessons.title: What a production system is
lessons.html:
The farm as a production system

A production system takes inputs, puts them through a process and produces outputs. On a farm:

InputsProcessOutputs
Land, water, seed, fertiliser, feed, animals, labour, machinery, fuel, money, knowledgePlanting, growing, feeding, milking, harvesting, packingMaize, milk, weaners, eggs, fruit; also by-products like manure and crop residues

There is also feedback: the results tell the farmer what to change next time, for example less fertiliser on a block that had good yields but high costs.

Types of farm production systems

  • Extensive – large areas, few inputs per hectare. Example: cattle or sheep on natural veld in the Karoo or bushveld.
  • Intensive – small areas, high inputs and high output per hectare. Example: broiler houses, feedlots, hydroponic tunnels, irrigated vegetables.
  • Mixed farming – crops and livestock on one farm, for example maize and cattle where cattle graze the maize stover in winter.
  • Subsistence – mainly produces food for the household.
  • Commercial – mainly produces for sale.
  • Organic and conservation agriculture – systems with special rules for inputs and soil management.

Parts of the system working together

All parts affect each other. If the feed supply in a dairy is poor, milk drops, cows lose condition, fertility falls and next year's calves and milk also suffer. A production system works best when every part is planned and balanced.

The production cycle

Most farm enterprises follow a cycle. For a maize crop: prepare land, plant, fertilise, control weeds and pests, harvest, store or sell. For a beef herd: mating, pregnancy, calving, raising calves, weaning, selling weaners. Knowing the cycle helps plan when inputs, labour and money are needed.

lessons.title: Managing production
lessons.html:
What production management is

Production management means planning, organising and controlling the production process so that the farm produces the right amount, of the right quality, at the right time, at the lowest reasonable cost.

1. Planning

  • Decide what to produce and how much, for example 20 ha of cabbages for a buyer in town.
  • Draw up a calendar: when to plant, fertilise, spray and harvest.
  • Work out inputs needed: seedlings, fertiliser, chemicals, water, labour, machinery hours.
  • Make a budget of costs and expected income.

2. Organising

  • Order inputs in time, so seedlings and fertiliser are on the farm when needed.
  • Make sure tractors and irrigation are serviced.
  • Allocate workers and supervisors to tasks.

3. Implementing

Carry out the work according to the plan and good practice, with attention to timing. A late planting or a delayed spray can cost much of the yield.

4. Controlling

  • Measure what is happening: growth, pest counts, milk yield, weights, costs.
  • Compare with the plan and the standard.
  • Correct problems early.
  • Keep records.

Quality and efficiency

Production management also looks at:

  • Quality – meeting the buyer's standard, for example size, colour and freedom from damage for fruit, or hygiene for milk.
  • Efficiency – producing more output for each unit of input, such as more kilograms of beef per kilogram of feed, or more tonnes per hectare for the same fertiliser.
  • Waste – reducing losses during harvest, storage and transport.
  • Sustainability – looking after soil, water and veld so the system keeps producing in future.

Example

A broiler farmer plans six batches a year. For each batch she orders chicks and feed, cleans and disinfects the house, checks water and temperature daily, weighs sample birds weekly and compares them with the target growth curve. When birds fall behind, she checks feed, water and ventilation and corrects the problem.

Key points

  • A production system turns inputs through a process into outputs, with feedback.
  • Systems can be extensive, intensive, mixed, subsistence or commercial.
  • All parts of the system affect each other.
  • Production management means planning, organising, implementing and controlling.
  • Aim for the right quantity and quality, on time, efficiently and sustainably.
